In specific simulations of alanine dipeptide (covering both vacuum and solvated conditions), our results demonstrate superior accuracy achieved with extended timesteps, without sacrificing computational efficiency or conformational exploration rates. Overall, this study offers broad practical guidance on simulating biologically relevant dynamics using the Langevin algorithm to boost the precision, reliability, and quantification of sampling.

We introduce a novel method for computing a specific type of eigenvector centrality applicable to multilayer networks subject to cross-layer constraints on node significance. These networks consist of multiple layers—each an edge-weighted and potentially directed graph sharing the same set of nodes—but lack direct inter-layer connections. Similar to classic eigenvector centrality, a node's importance within a layer depends on the weighted relevance of its neighbors within that same layer. However, unlike the standard model, we allow both the adjacency relations and the importance values to be influenced by different layers. Crucially, existing multilayer centrality frameworks utilizing explicit inter-layer dependencies only partially support such constrained, layer-specific requirements. In our proposed model, these constraints define centrality scores through a combination of independent eigenvalue problems and dependent multilayer eigenvalue problems, which can be solved to optimality via an efficient iterative algorithm.

Multielectron quantum dots, or ensemble quantum dots, represent a promising path toward advancing mini and integrated optical technologies. Researchers have established strong interactions between these systems and light, showcasing efficient single-photon statistics, fast and deterministic on-demand emission, and scalable production. Nevertheless, current benchmarks still trail those achieved by traditional single quantum dots. In response, this study details the development of thicker, vertical multielectron quantum dots built on a membrane-based platform. These improvements significantly enhance lifetime product quality and substantially boost collection efficiency—reaching 74%—by leveraging dark excitons. Compared to bright excitons, dark excitons offer smaller divergence, higher damage resistance, and inherently lower temperatures. Additionally, these multielectron dots exhibit remarkable stability; they maintained consistent performance after over 100 laser-correcting operations, involving more than a billion single laser corrections, confirming their durability. This combination of high-quality and durability in multielectron nodes paves the way for reliable, long-term scalable nodes. With further improvements, these systems are well on track to exceed the single-node performance benchmarks demonstrated here. These findings highlight that multielectron nodes can now meet the performance requirements of single-node systems. These findings also indicate multi-electron systems are ideal for future developments.

Using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding framework incorporating horizontal and vertical hopping, we identify two inequivalent Dirac cones located along a specific high-symmetry path in the first Brillouin zone. These findings enhance the understanding of Dirac materials by demonstrating that even the most complex 2D arrangements can support Dirac fermions. Because these states of matter are protected by crystallographic symmetries, highlighting their robustness through a unit cell possessing no internal symmetry is a significant contribution. Such systems therefore offer promising candidates for directing Dirac states with high precision.

Defined as advanced capability in two or more languages for both spoken and written communication, multilingualism frequently manifests through code-switching or code-mixing within individual sentences. This work reviews existing natural language processing (NLP) literature regarding its limitations and obstacles when addressing five critical social impact areas: crisis response, healthcare support, political engagement, anti-disinformation strategies, and hate speech mitigation in multilingual communities. Furthermore, we introduce prospective datasets, models, and utilities poised to propel multilingual NLP research toward broader societal benefits. Utilizing English-Hindi mixing as a case study allows for applicable insights across broader scenarios involving languages shared by substantial speaker populations globally.

Automatic image description models are typically built and assessed on crowd-sourced human references, with the top-performing system selected by measuring similarity against these references using metrics such as BLEU, CIDER, or METEOR. Consequently, since both system performance and evaluation accuracy hinge on these descriptions, ensuring their high quality and diversity is critical. Given that acquiring diverse, accurate descriptions through manual annotation of new datasets is costly and labor-intensive, this study proposes leveraging Large Language Models to generate descriptions for any image. To specifically enhance the diversity of the cluster-based description variety captured in traditional evaluation protocols—which are distinct from sentence-level diversity—we conducted a re-evaluation of the diversity of references using the TF - IDF approach. Furthermore, we introduced a refined classifier to identify and remove duplicate descriptions, applying this enhanced framework to the standard single-label classification used for system performance comparison. Evaluations across three datasets—the MS-COCO test split, object recognition tasks like NYU-Object360 and Object360, and the Visual Genome benchmark demonstrate that utilizing AI-generated references via our method significantly boosts the measured performance of current description models while maintaining a strong correlation with human-reference-based benchmarks, confirming that AI-generated references serve as a practical solution for image description tasks.

Tantalum oxides (Ta$_2$O$_5$) exhibit favorable physical and chemical traits, including strong antireflective capabilities and high dielectric constants. In addition, recent studies suggest that Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles could enhance biological efficacy in cancer hadron therapy, and first-principles simulations offer a robust method for exploring their electronic properties. However, the multiplicity of stable polymorphs poses a significant obstacle to conventional simulation protocols. To address this challenge, we apply a hybrid functional approach using WIEN2k for our calculations. As an outcome, we present the unrestricted density functional theory (DFT) results regarding the magnetic and structural characteristics of each tantalum oxide phase. The computed total energies were integrated with the USPEFF algorithm to predict room-temperature stable phases of Ta$_2$O$_5$, and the resulting dataset was used to train a neural network. Finally, our phenomenological model provides accurate predictions for the spectral functions of all polymorphs, covering the entire valence region.

Previous studies mostly attributed the spread of online misinformation to individual traits or specific misinformation tactics alone, neglecting the influence of geographic context and its interaction with those top-down approaches. This research investigates whether such falsehoods circulate differently across U.S. states, specifically examining the moderating effect of state-level conscientiousness on this spread. Analyzing ten years worth of data from the AllFact project reveals that, consistent with prior work, actively promoting misinformation increases its reach; however, this strategy's efficacy varies significantly by location. Specifically, this approach is significantly less effective in states characterized by higher levels of conscientiousness. We argue that understanding the geospatial dimensions of misinformation ecosystems is crucial for developing targeted interventions designed to reduce the impact of these narratives.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has gained significant interest from researchers for its potential to mitigate data sparsity in recommender systems. Nevertheless, existing single- or dual-target CDR techniques frequently face limitations, including the requirement that at least one domain contains sufficient data and their strong reliance on domain-invariant preferences. These assumptions are often unrealistic in scenarios where sparsity is widespread. To address these challenges, we propose MSDCR (Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation), a multi-sparse-domain approach designed to enhance user preference prediction by integrating assumptions that vary across domains. MSDCR simultaneously leverages abundant preference data from domain A and sparse data from domain B, in addition to the more complex assumption of domain-specific preferences. By targeting domain-sutter preferences, the method effectively overcomes data limitations found in multiple domains. Empirical results across three datasets confirm that our approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation baselines.

Convex optimization encompasses a broad spectrum of mathematical models, ranging from basic quadratic and linear programs up to intricate second-order and cone programs. In this paper, we introduce a methodology for defining and employing exotic cones in such problems. These cones arise from taking the intersection of multiple, distinct cone types with possibly different dimensions and applying specific linear transformations during this combination. We delineate the algorithms required for working with exotic cones and demonstrate the approach by showing how it naturally accommodates the representation of fourth-order cones and skew products of cones.

Rapidly advancing automated quality control (QC) systems for MRI rely on deep learning to offer clinical benefits, yet generalizing these models remains a significant hurdle. This study evaluates the generalization capabilities of several popular automated QC networks across three distinct datasets: two Multi-Parametric MRI collections from different centers (each comprising roughly 1,000 scans) and a third set composed by splitting one center's data into training and testing groups (n=973). The authors compare evaluations between shared learning from third-party and local groups versus sole third-party training, utilizing both ranking- and regression-based assessment techniques enhanced by visual analysis to identify causes for variability. They find that although splitting assessments by source improves performance, it still trails significantly behind a single learning source, with issues worsening as the third-party dataset diverges. Moreover, they assess whether assessment design and key metrics impact overall results quality and suggest next phases for improving assessment accuracy.

This paper examines the impact of privately owned electric vehicles on power system stability during disruptions. To capture the decentralized interactions within transportation and energy domains, we introduce a Network-based Multi-Agent Optimization with Equilibrium Constraints (N-MOPEC) framework. Specifically designed for a high-dimensional non-convex problem, our solution employs a specialized algorithm relying on precise convex reformulation. Extensive numerical experiments validate both the proposed methodology's efficacy in visualization and its potential policy ramifications, establishing a robust basis to advance resilience research on integrated transportation-power networks influenced by private EVs.

This study investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn$_3$, CmSn$_3$, and the solid solution Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ series ($x$ = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75). The calculations employ the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation framework. Bulk ground-state properties for all three components (GdSn$_3$ and CmSn$_3$) and their intermediate phases are analyzed in detail to characterize phase evolution across the entire series. Results indicate that both GdSn$_3$ and CmSn$_3$ are antiferromagnetic metals. Furthermore, substituting Gd with Cm alters key properties such as lattice constants, unit cell volume, and magnetic susceptibility. This paper offers a strict mathematical analysis of word2vec neural network models, specifically examining their connection to term statistics within a text corpus. We identify and reconcile these algorithms with the Skip-Bigram Model, utilizing this model to derive closed-form solutions for both the "Slow" (hierarchical) and "Fast" (hierarchical) training variants. This work introduces MG-GLAM, software specifically designed to generate full-scale cosmological $N$-body simulations within a wide range of modified gravity (MG) frameworks. The code employs a standard particle-mesh (PM) approach, augmented by a higher-order multigrid correction to handle short wavelengths and has been validated against various analytical probes and simulation data. Significantly, multigrid feedback enables the use of sufficiently small resolution scales to accurately resolve dark matter halo structures and formation processes. The software supports grid-based implementations of MG modifications, facilitating rigorous testing of major models, including cubic $f(R)$ gravity, $\phi$- $F(R)$ gravity, Bimetric $G_{\Lambda}$, and cubic $f(R)$ gravity. In addition to standard output metrics such as particle and mesh data, the tool facilitates real-time computation of observational proxies. A prominent feature is the capability to self-consistently incorporate MG effects in the simulation of galaxy formation physics via Subgrid Physics (SP) models. Consequently, feedback mechanisms can be calibrated using star formation simulations in Milky Way-like atomic hydrogen ($R$) simulations, allowing researchers to apply these parameters directly in full-scale cosmological N-body simulations. Significant efforts have been devoted to calibrating the software for these subgrid physics applications.

This investigation conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent, methane-fuelled, atmospheric jet to forecast how the flow reacts to upstream acoustic actuation. Capturing heat release variations is essential for understanding thermoacoustic instabilities and flame acoustic signatures within a linear theory. Distinct from prior research, this work employs active combustion theories to integrate flame heat release oscillations triggered by acoustic signals, requiring that the combustion model be linearized. Although linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models introduces closure issues, rendering their application problematic in this context, Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these difficulties and emerge as appropriate choices. These models were linearized around the time-averaged characteristics of the simulated jet, which itself was computed using LES. The findings demonstrate that key parameters—including acoustic intensity, distance from the source, and the combustion model itself—influence how acoustic packet waves trigger heat release oscillations and how those oscillations interact acoustically. Notably, the computed response functions stay consistent with those derived from LES, particularly when the jet is operated in a far-field acoustic environment.

In this paper, I provide a representative, non-exhaustive overview of selected high-energy physics (HEP) systems and questions at the core of my research. Specifically, I focus on the efforts led by the PHENIX collaboration at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) to detect and analyze collective behavior in high-momentum-transport, small-scale systems. Rotation can significantly impact whether hydrogen sustains burning in very low-mass stellar bodies. This occurs in two ways: by altering hydrostatic balance through centrifugal force and by reaching the mass-shedding limit where rotation causes break-up. Our numerical models explore rotating very low-mass stellar objects that either sustain nuclear fusion as their energy source or do not, with an emphasis on scenarios involving high rotation speeds and the consequent structural changes, including those triggered by nuclear ignition conditions varying with spin and angular momentum losses leading to disruption through mass shedding. Our findings indicate that both disruptive breakdown and nuclear ignition thresholds are met when the equator rotates to roughly 60 percent of the critical break-up rate; however, radius changes due to central density shifts in non-fusion objects are negligible until the 60 percent threshold is crossed, whereas radii in objects that do sustain burning contract as rotation increases, potentially skewing observational interpretations of limiting densities used to define formation criteria; the theoretical curves generated here, which relate radius against mass under diverse spin conditions, offer a method for distinguishing between limiting density values derived from observations that involve objects with substantial rotational influence.

By integrating this approach with junction tree inference, we achieve more efficient and effective performance. Additionally, we establish the theoretical connection between finite state automata and Markov factor graphs. It is important to distinguish this work from previous efforts that used tiled matrix configurations; our method is unique because it employs deterministic finite state automata and offers a non-reversible representation scheme. Furthermore, since tile-based techniques rely on reversing transformations to execute forward passes (such as in CNN computation using tiled junction trees), our irreversible deterministic finite state approach eliminates the need for such reversals. Testing on various scenarios—including standard junction tree inference, reverse-mode automatic differentiation (RDAD), and forward-pass CNN inference—demonstrates that our method is both effective and competitive, achieving a 100x reduction in memory usage for ViT back propagation without impacting performance.

Non-rigid registration stands as a fundamental technique in soft-tissue navigation, specifically within laparoscopic liver surgery. Our work addresses the challenge of mapping a preoperative CT-derived organ model onto the intraoperative surface of the liver, reconstructed from surgical camera feeds. These tasks are inherently difficult due to noisy and limited real-time data, the critical need for immediate processing, and multiple ambiguous factors such as tissue behavior and boundary constraints. Additionally, aligning pre-operative and intra-operative data poses a significant hurdle; this is largely because liver tissues typically possess few distinct surface markers, while the surgical images often suffer from low resolution, resulting in high noise levels.

These issues collectively inform the design of a particularly streamlined pipeline. This framework integrates organ deformable modeling with visual data to train a fully automatic network named WGAN-DM. The proposed framework relies on two interconnected modules: the first employs depth-aware image priorization to link visual inputs to point clouds representing the deformable model, whereas the second utilizes the geometric constraints and deformation fields calculated from those point clouds as prior knowledge to refine alignment. This process is refined through adversarial training mechanisms and the incorporation of terms that measure both flow conservation and the preservation of organ volume.

Simulation studies and practical deployment on real-world data demonstrate that the WGAN-DM architecture consistently outperformed leading alternative algorithms. Its superior performance stems from high interpretability, rapid computation speeds, and consistently accurate outcomes.

A graph $G$ exhibits the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian (PMH) property if every one of its perfect matchings can be paired with another perfect matching such that their union forms a Hamiltonian cycle. Research into graphs satisfying this condition, which began in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, explores the intersections of edge colourings, matchings, and Hamiltonicity. Our study focuses on cubic graphs. We demonstrate that under the condition where girth is strictly greater than 6—or if no bipartite subgraph comprises 2 vertices, 4 edges, and 9 edges—every cyclically 4-coloured cubic graph with an even number of edges possesses the PMH-property. Additionally, we introduce and analyse a generalisation of 3-edge colouring applicable to odd cycles.

We introduce Timeloops, a novel approach for the automatic generation of system call filtering policies aimed at containerized microservices. At runtime, this system learns permissible system calls for programs while rejecting those invoking spurious operations. The method imposes no assumptions regarding application architecture, source or compiled availability, programming languages, system calls, or specific failure modes. Our technique is evaluated using a broad selection of open-source applications; the resulting polarized filtering rules effectively reject superfluous system calls to effect time erors. When contrasted with static analysis-based methods, the learned filters achieved a 93% reduction in policy size for a typical system of microservices while maintaining an average 2.8-fold improvement in rejection speed per operation. When compared to existing runtime verification tools, Timeloops operated 2.3x faster in system call rejection processes across the board of applications tested.

Soccer is a sparsely rewarded activity where strategic choices during pivotal moments significantly influence the outcome, creating a need for playing styles adaptable to various game states. This study examines whether a neural network trained on critical gameplay scenarios of soccer learns to prioritize high-scoring moves, even though such actions may involve compromising ball possession, by evaluating different potential optimal strategies. Three potential optimal behaviors were investigated within the context of the neural network training process. Our results indicate that the network likely achieves greater cumulative scores by focusing on immediate utility for each move, rather than utilizing the standard total game outcome as its learning signal, effectively neglecting the influence of final victory or defeat during training.

Full waveform inversion (FWI), which enhances initial subsurface models by contrasting synthetic and observed data, suffers as a nonlinear optimizer that can become stuck at local minima despite its potential for high-resolution imaging. Our approach introduces a storage-efficient variant, which we term single-source wavefield reconstruction inversion (SS-WRI), designed specifically to eliminate the excessive overhead. Traditional WRI necessitates retaining three sources of data sources per frequency: forward-propagated wavefields, their adjoints, and iteratively refined backward wavefields generated through matches at receiver points. While the first two require storage proportional to the square of the number of spatial and time samples, previous methods required the third to consume memory equivalent to twice that of the first two, creating prohibitive costs. In contrast, our memory-optimized strategy stores only the source terms, requiring minimal additional space. By integrating these techniques, the method drastically cuts the footprint needed for wavefield equations, rendering large-scale computations feasible. Tested on both synthetic and real-world datasets, this improved algorithm delivers consistent convergence and confirms superior performance relative to existing standards.

Radiation constraints inherent to positron emission tomography (PET) imaging hinder its application for studying vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, children, adults needing frequent scans. Empirical results drawn from simultaneous in vivo PET-MRI and various types of OOD datasets demonstrate both superior quantitative and qualitative performance of suDNN over current benchmarks.

Centering Theory (Grosz et al., 1995) analyzes how the structural components of conversation maintain local coherence through successive utterances referencing shared entities. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that pretrained context-aware embeddings inherently encode much of this coherence information, which likely explains why Centering Theory yields minimal improvements for models using such representations. We propose an adapted version of CT incorporating recency bias, demonstrating that it more accurately captures coreference patterns than the unmodified theory.

Accurately and quickly predicting river flow velocities is critical for various applications, such as managing flood risks. Qualitative analysis indicates that these models excel at capturing where viscous influences occur and how they propagate within the water. Consequently, machine learning approaches offer a robust alternative for real-time, near-shore flow prediction.

This paper examines the reasons behind the high false positive rate in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). The study highlights that the training procedure is the primary source of these positives, caused by an imbalance in relationship proposal lengths. Specifically, genuine object pairs have short sequences, whereas single-object proposals and false-positive proposals are significantly longer. These extended sequences allow adversarial samples more opportunities to introduce noise that mimics valid object pairs, disrupting training despite proposal filtering. The authors introduce two affordable techniques during data generation and proposal sampling to equalize sequence lengths, ensuring balanced batching during training without requiring retraining. Proposals are padded to match the longest sequence in each batch, with extra tokens having neutral attention to preserve balance. However, such proposal counts and object detection rates vary widely across different test images, resulting in uneven batch compositions regarding sequence length distribution. Furthermore, prior sampling methods that fix average lengths often generate large batches dominated by padding, which degrades performance. The suggested solution is "Length-Proportional Sampling," an approach weighting samples by their proposal count for a target average length and proportionate batch sizes, avoiding excessive padding while maintaining balance. The dataset provided by these innovations shows heightened false-positive signals from object detectors, yet GQA and Cohendy benchmarks indicate that relationship detection tasks benefit from balanced training proposals, confirming that training imbalances driven by proposal length imbalances adversely impact model performance.

Feature extraction offers a viable strategy to mitigate dimensionality challenges within high-dimensional datasets. As a prevalent self-supervised learning technique, contrastive learning has recently attracted substantial interest. In this research, we introduced a unified framework grounded in a novel interpretation of contrastive learning, applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework first establishes two contrastive (CL) graphs to distinctly identify positive and negative pairs; subsequently, the projection matrix is obtained by minimizing the corresponding contrastive loss function to integrate information from both similar and dissimilar examples for enhancing extraction performance. Furthermore, because the proposed framework is not restricted by label constraints, it proves particularly effective in scenarios involving unsupervised feature extraction. Finally, empirical evaluations across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the framework's superior performance when compared to several baseline methods.

Model selection or sparse modelling for categorical variables remains problematic, even with a moderate variable count, as encoding each category requires a parameter, quickly leading to non-solutions. Although Group Lasso is an established and efficient tool for selecting continuous or categorical variables, its estimates for individual levels of selected factors are rarely identical. Because of the lack uniformity, resulting models often fail to achieve true sparsity, hindering interpretability. We address this by proposing a two-stage strategy: initially, dimensionality is reduced using Group Lasso; subsequently, final selection is made over a narrowed candidate space via an information criterion applied to clusters of factor levels constructed after the initial selection phase. We examine algorithm accuracy within sparse, high-dimensional contexts, applying our approach to both synthetic examples and realistic datasets, demonstrating that our methods generally outperform current-state-of-the-art algorithms regarding prediction accuracy or model size efficiency at the variable dimension.

Knowledge distillation serves as a proven strategy for expediting deep neural networks, wherein a smaller "student" model mimics the soft probability outputs of a large "teacher" network. Traditionally, this process requires access to both the input training data and the internal parameters of the white-box teacher transfer; however, constraints such as storage limits or privacy concerns in practical deployments often make these prerequisites unattainable. This work introduces Decision-based Black-Box (DB3) knowledge distillation, a technique that trains a student model by extracting knowledge exclusively from a teacher where parameters are inaccessible and decisions are revealed only as final class labels, without softmax probabilities. Initially, we address settings where training data remains available: we estimate a sample's robustness by measuring its distance to the teacher's decision boundaries, utilizing these metrics to generate soft labels for standard distillation. Furthermore, we address the more demanding case wherein even training data access is blocked by proposing a transfer dataset constructed from synthetic samples that are maximally distinguished by the teacher; these samples receive generated soft labels to facilitate training. Evaluations across multiple datasets and networks validate the efficacy of these methods. Source code can be obtained at https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd/.

Imitation learning primarily enhances reinforcement learning efficiency by utilizing expert demonstrations. Speech-emotion recognition (SER) empowers computers to interact emotionally intelligently. Detecting fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), often called anisotropies, is among the most vital techniques in cosmological research. Due to the faintness of this signal, scientists have built ever more sophisticated and sensitive instruments capable of scanning the sky across multiple frequencies with thousands of detectors sensitive to polarization. As these experiments reach higher levels of sensitivity, instrumental artifacts are often becoming the primary obstacle to fully realizing their data potential. We introduce *s4cmb* (Systematics for CMB), a Python toolkit designed to generate raw, bolometric-based time-domain data streams for current-generation CMB missions while realistically inserting instrumental systematic effects. *s4cmb* aims not only to evaluate the impact of such systematics on actual datasets and to inform the architecture of future detectors but also to create more authentic simulations essential for refining analytical methodologies.

Word reordering represents a language generation challenge where models must arrange unordered inputs into coherent text using ordered output, based primarily on existing studies employing standard models or neural networks. Despite this history, researchers have not yet investigated the potential of large, word-oriented language models or exploited the extensive benefits derivable from billion-parameter architectures trained on vast word-ordering datasets. To address these issues, we conducted comprehensive experiments with relatively small-scale datasets utilizing the open-source BART model to assess its performance on two word reordering tasks and explore potential enhancements through data augmentation. The first task involved answering open-ended questions, while the second mapped textual sentiment; both significantly surpassed baseline results by wide margins when compared against existing baselines. Ultimately, we observed significant improvements derived primarily from BART's superior performance on word-order augmentation tasks thanks to its strong mastery of linguistically ordered knowledge.

Community detection poses significant challenges yet remains highly relevant across diverse fields, encompassing everything from power grids and atmospheric science to social and financial networks. However, addressing these issues in many dynamic systems is often difficult because the inherent complexity makes deriving traditional mathematical models for clustering impractical. Furthermore, effective clustering of dynamic systems must explicitly consider their temporal behavior. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel methodology for clustering dynamical systems using only raw time-series data, thereby inherently capturing the underlying dynamics. This approach defines a distance or similarity metric between states by integrating the distances between their respective attractors. Most attractors within a class can be represented by their generic orbits, known as skeletons. Consequently, this new framework operates on the assumption that generic orbits serve as representative structures. We evaluate the framework initially with standard synthetic datasets and subsequently apply it to detect communities among three dynamic, data-rich, real-world datasets: the US Congress dataset, the MacFlu dataset, and the Wikipedia dataset.

Implementing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiability of the full training loop, a limitation existing approaches address poorly with either inaccurate gradient estimates or poor-quality sentence embeddings. Drawing inspiration from sparse coding, we introduce SparseGAN to feed sparse, semantically meaningful sentence representations to the discriminator. This is achieved by treating the embedding matrix as an over-complete dictionary, approximating generator output features at each timestep through a linear combination of only a few selected word embeddings. These robust semantic representations streamline adversarial learning and ensure full differentiability, while empirical results across multiple datasets demonstrate performance gains, particularly improving BLEU scores for whole sequences.

The concept that life can migrate across planetary systems, known as interstellar panspermia, dates back decades but remains hard to validate through observation. To evaluate the chances of confirming this phenomenon, we established a mathematical framework accounting for factors such as the lifespan of resilient microbes in transit, the dispersion of stellar velocities, and the distribution of ejected material. We find that the key dimensionless parameter governing this issue is the ratio between the wandering semi-radius of the ejected population and the maximum distance reached by interstellar travelers. When the latter is significant, the average time an individual object remains habitable drops markedly, yet this specific scenario is rare in practice. For typical cases where it is not the dominant factor, our equations offer a means to estimate the intrinsic velocity dispersion based on measured mean residence times for habitability. Furthermore, we observe that the symmetric, "Hoyle-type" mechanism—characterized by objects moving at negative relative velocities—is exceptionally effective at satisfying observational tests. In contrast, mechanisms generating high velocity dispersions present stricter challenges. Finally, we apply these relations to several proposed interstellar objects, including those hypothesized to support panspermia.

Accurate traffic control depends on effectively estimating traffic states. This research proposes an integrative, nonparametric technique for short-term queue length estimation, utilizing partial queue length observations on a 15-minute basis. The approach begins with the assumption that queue lengths adhere to either a normal or lognormal distribution conditioned on traffic demand. It then employs Bayesian methods to derive these conditional distributions: first establishing conditional and marginal probabilities for specific observation types based on calibration against known distributions, and subsequently applying identical parameters to new conditioning scenarios regardless of original data context. At intersections lacking existing queue monitoring infrastructure—such as the majority analyzed here—the method substitutes standard observations with data on passing probe vehicles. Validation across nine intersections in Los Angeles demonstrates the technique's reliability; notably, accurate estimates were achieved even at under-saturated intersections primarily by leveraging the normal distribution assumption, supported by substantial empirical evidence. The study confirms that this framework delivers robust state estimation for traffic intersections with minimal computational complexity.

Numerical relativity simulations involving non-trivial matter configurations require solving the ADM Hamiltonian and momentum constraints to determine initial metric data. This study introduces a novel method grounded in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Rather than treating mean curvature ($K$) as a fixed value and solving the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation, this new scheme involves selecting a specific conformal factor to derive $K$ via an algebraic equation. This approach circumvents the challenges posed by solution existence and uniqueness issues associated with the elliptic constraint, doing so without resorting to the typical rescaling of source terms, a feature that is especially crucial when simulating scenarios like charged black holes. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, the paper demonstrates that this technique yields high precision for various charged black hole configurations characterized by significant net charge and distinct separations, when evaluated against direct comparisons within exact analytical solutions. Performance metrics include typical numerical errors below one part in $10^2$ and a convergence rate of roughly two orders of magnitude per iteration across diverse initial distances and charge distributions. The final metric data produced exhibits several physical attributes, notably confirming the impossibility of net charge existing on an uncharged black hole. Furthermore, the study utilizes these results to simulate several dynamical scenarios with substantial electromagnetic fields and large $|K|$, including scalar star configurations, double black hole systems, and scalar stars endowed with significant net charge.

The resurgence in research regarding magnetic materials that display a significant anomalous Hall effect despite negligible magnetization stems from the desire to control and understand these phenomena. Antiferromagnetic materials within the antiperovskite structure are a developing class unique for diverse properties derived from their intricate electronic bands and magnetic arrangements; however, reports quantifying the anomalous Nernst effect in this group remain scarce. This limitation is partially attributed to the difficulty in accurately extracting the anomalous Nernst coefficient through experiments. Addressing this, we present new experimental findings on the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN antiferromagnetic antiperovkslite thin films. By utilizing the same sample geometry and current configurations for both Hall and Nernst measurements, we demonstrate a straightforward method to extract unambiguous ANE coefficients. With this approach, we quantify the Seebeck, normal Nernst, and anomalous Nernst effects in Mn$_3$NiN at low temperatures, achieving peak ANE values of roughly 12 $\mu\Omega$/K$^2$ at 5 K. Finally, we discuss these results alongside other recent studies to clarify the underlying mechanisms driving the anomalous Nernst response in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites.

As such, skML serves as a foundational framework for creating more advanced applications in experiment management.

While static graphs function well when a system's connectivity remains unchanged, dynamic systems involve time-evolving relationships that static models often fail to capture accurately—particularly their division into connected components. A primary obstacle in creating diverse graphs over time is the non-dissimilar similarity between neighboring nodes; traditional similarity metrics also struggle with noise and outliers. Addressing this, we introduce a new system that automatically builds a dynamic graph by integrating a discrete map with multiple localized similarity graphs, each representing different graph connectivity regions. This approach leverages the map to provide global structure and employ dimension-specific similarity charts to maintain precise local connections, thereby enabling the resulting time-dependent graph to rigorously reflect actual system dynamics regarding how connected partitions form, split, or transition through transitions. The system successfully tracks these variations in partition topology while preserving local structural integrity, as demonstrated by simulations comparing our method against state-of-the-art approaches.

Animals move to achieve various goals, including finding mates, securing food, escaping predators, and navigating changing environments. Therefore, analyzing how locomotion aids biological adaptation is crucial. Although general theories on biological movement exist, a specific framework for insect motion has been lacking. This study focuses on *Blaptica dubia* (dubrova cockroaches) to examine diverse movement types, ranging from simple actions like walking and running to complex behaviors such as escaping, foraging, and exploring new spaces.

To facilitate the investigation, we categorized these movements based on distinct kinematic indicators: velocity, acceleration, and particularly directional changes or turning angles. Our findings suggest that directional change is the most reliable metric for differentiating between various locomotor activities in *B. dubia*. Summaringly, we have established and described several movement patterns in this species, validated through statistical analysis and supported by existing biological literature. These movements were classified as follows: walking and running by high intensities; escaping and foraging by combinations of escalating acceleration alongside frequent reorientation; and simple exploration (SD) versus complex, motivated exploration (CE) based on how the frequency of reorientation increases with the level of environmental motivation.

Ultimately, this work demonstrates how linking animals to their habitats allows for clearer definitions and distinctions in their movements. By applying this adaptive context to *B. dubia*, different modes of motion were successfully identified through objective physical metrics rather than subjective visual assessment alone.

The findings reveal that spatial randomness and binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter ranges. Within this topological Anderson insulator regime, the bulk states localization, constrained by system size, is managed by tuning the expansion of system space. Furthermore, edge states are identified to display distinct dynamics: their behavior is influenced by system expansion, correlates with bulk states randomness, remains sensitive to system size, but is independent of lattice length orientation in this context. Utilizing the mathematical framework of Chern numbers and by analyzing the behavior of conductance systems, the study establishes clear distinctions between the topological Anderson Mott insulator and the trivial anderson insulator. Additionally, the study observes that the boundary states in this system can cross over into the topological anderson insulator through specific correlations of binary disorder, space randomization. In conclusion, the study notes that system size expansion can determine the transition parameters between the co-existing trivial and non-trivial bulk states insulation.

We present findings from an application of Event Shape Engineering in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm{NN}}}=2.76$ TeV. Events were sorted within the same centrality class but with varying degrees of flow, allowing for an examination of different initial geometric configurations. The study demonstrates that event-shape selection influences the elliptic flow coefficient ($v_2$) independently of transverse momentum (${p_\rm{T}}$); this $ {p_\rm{T}}$ dependence, however, serves as a sensitive indicator of selected events. Consequently, the measured differential elliptic flow enables the characterization of engineered initial geometries and validates initial state models capable of describing early collision dynamics and subsequent evolution consistent with Pb-Pb interactions at the LHC. Furthermore, initial conditions derived from such models and the observed $ {p_\rm{T}}$ dependence of $v_2$ suggest that increasing the reaction plane angle for a given impact parameter enhances particle yields, a phenomenon directly relevant to the improved yield of double charmonium states at high $ {p_\rm{T}}$ in Pb-Pb collisions relative to proton-proton collisions.

This paper investigates the maximum performance improvement achieved by optimal power control compared to binary (on/off) schemes within large interference networks. Leveraging Extremum Theory and the Poisson Point Process (PPP), we establish that this optimal gain converges as a deterministic value when network density increases indefinitely. Numerical simulations confirm this convergence across both PPP and grid-based deployments. Crucially, the limiting value exhibits exponential scaling relative to the square root of the number of users, implying that binary power controls fail to track the capacity growth of modern systems. Furthermore, this limit exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the path-loss exponent and is notably sensitive initial conditions of the power control algorithm. Despite the effectiveness of the proposed heuristic, multiple distinct realizations yield an identical extremal performance, regardless of their underlying base station configurations.

This paper introduces a Multi-Time-Step (MTS) approach to resolve numerical instability caused by the stiff interaction between particle motion and fluid dynamics time scales. Traditional methods that artificially increase the particle time step to align with the fluid step have shown limitations; specifically, the prior "collision time" technique caused particles to accumulate unnatural velocities between steps, negatively impacting entrainment rates. Our proposed method decouples the particle solution domain into two components: one with a larger time step containing implicit sub-cycles for handling stiff operations (such as collisions), and one with a smaller time step dedicated to coupling with the fluid solver. This avoids imparting excessive inter-step velocities while accurately managing collisions and maintaining a strict time-consistent coupling between phases. Validation against direct numerical simulation (DNS) data—covering both isolated particle dynamics and dense ensembles in channels—confirms that the new technique correctly captures impact timing and produces results consistent with per-particle DNS, including accurate collision handling. Crucially, it preserves physical outcomes for sediment entrainment and maintains consistent particle-fluid turbulence interactions when operating with large, computationally stiff time scales.

Locomotion utilizing legs on deformable ground represents a difficult and unresolved issue in robotic physics. The unpredictable dynamic behaviors caused by surface deformation significantly hinder the accuracy of both modeling techniques and control strategies. Furthermore, determining the optimal controls and mechanisms to ensure efficient and stable movement across soft terrains is particularly complex. Addressed below are three primary challenges within this domain: first, the limitations of existing predictive models and methods for managing ground deformation uncertainty; second, advancements in architectural designs suited for navigating such environments; and finally, developments in sensor technologies specifically for soft ground interaction.

This manuscript examines the determination of elastic meson form factors within a contact interaction model. Dressed masses for both quarks and mesons are established using gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations. Specifically, the general $M\gamma \to \text{elastic scattering }$ process, where M denotes a two-flavored meson, is analyzed, while charge radii are computed by explicitly evaluating the corresponding form factors for pseudoscalar, axial-vector, vector, and scalar states.

Information hierarchies typically function as structures to organize and display extensive, complex data while enabling efficient human navigation. Although numerous statistical and computational models exist for automating their generation, current methods often fail to account for links found in information {em networks}, which are ubiquitous in real-world settings. These approaches also usually depict topics as abstract probabilistic distributions, words, etc., failing to employ concrete network-derived nodes. Furthermore, the statistical methodologies in prior works often cannot manage data at Web-scale. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM); it computes nonparametric Bayesian models through a distributed vertex-programming process. Evaluations across three medium-scale datasets and the complete Wikipedia dataset demonstrate that HDTM successfully maps accurate topic hierarchies over large, extensive information networks.

Quenching and annealing represent opposing approaches to the time-evolution of quantum systems; annealing slowly adjusts a Hamiltonian's parameters to explore equilibrium phases for solving complex optimizations, while quenching imposes sudden changes that create non-equilibrium states. We examine the connection between both regimes, demonstrating that a dynamical quench parameter—which characterizes the post-quench quantum state—allows us to expose the minimum annealing gap. A key bottleneck for these algorithms, this hidden landscape becomes accessible when combined with statistical methods such as neural network training. These tools can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap using only quench-based data. We further propose that partial or complete knowledge of the obtained gap enables optimized quantum annealing strategies with tangible improvements in solution times. These predictions are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians used to represent computationally demanding problems like the 3-coloring of graphs and the simple exponential optimization problem.

The phase structure of dense matter accessed during core collapse and supernova explosions is investigated through a constitutive model where the sound velocity rises with density, reaching nearly $2 E/9n$ at extremely high levels, approximating one half of the speed of light. While this trend implies a degenerate quark-gas scenario that may not strictly reflect the dynamics within supranuclear density ranges, the model offers valuable insights regardless. Two distinct cases are analyzed based on state equations where the sound velocity approaches $E/3n$ and $\sqrt{2}E/3n$. For the quark-gas model ($c_s^2 = \omega = 2/3 E/3n$), no collapse occurs under central forces; however, solutions exist involving self-gravitating, strongly self-interacting systems. In contrast, when the pressure follows $p = \sqrt{2 E/3n^3}$, stable stationary states exist for spheres bounded both by gravitational attraction and strong surface forces, in addition to unbounded systems lacking such constraints.

No collapse occurs with attractive gravity alone under specific conditions, such as when $p = \sqrt{2 E/3n^3}$; however, the presence of strong self-repellent and purely gravitational forces yields diverse solutions. These configurations encompass degenerate stars composed of both fermions and bosons, as well as various quasi-star states.

We examine a diverse set of non-classical states formed from coherent states subject to squeezing and displacement operations. Within the framework of Heisenberg scaling analysis, we determine the optimal parameters for these states specifically for estimating both the squeezing and displacement parameters. Using a simple linear model, our investigation assesses the practical performance of the measurement and data processing techniques on realistic conditions containing experimental noise. A key outcome identifies distinct applications for particular states: enhanced sensitivity beyond that of coherent states is achieved by adjusting only the squeezing, whereas concurrent modification of both squeezing and shifting yields results that are largely uncorrelated errors in displacement estimation despite precise squeezing evaluation, all in relation to maximum-likelihood estimation performance.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) involves hydrodynamical processes requiring swift gas cooling; it is posited to function in the outer sectors of protoplanetary disks. Although the VSI generates vertical turbulent motions capable of influencing dust accumulation and sinking, dust dynamics can conversely dampen the instability: reduced gas opacity due to dust removal hampers cooling in the already thin outer regions. Utilizing linear analysis, this research quantifies how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. By devising a cooling timescale model that accounts for dust maturation beyond one micron and size-dependent sedimentation, we integrate it with linear stability analysis to determine VSI activity regions (the "VSI zones") and their peak growth rates at various radii. Results indicate that dust maturation and sinking confine the VSI zone more tightly along the midplane, resulting in reduced growth rates due to diminished shear in the vertically weaker velocity fields near the lower disk altitudes. Specifically, for a 0.01 solar mass disk, allowing dust to grow from 10 microns to 1 mm suppresses growth rates by an order of magnitude exceeding 10. Consequently, dust-driven turbulence suppression likely facilitates additional outer-disk dust evolution and accounts for the pronounced settling seen in the HL Tau system.

The rise of outsourcing training and Machine Learning-as-a-Service services has introduced novel attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks, which embed secret functionality into neural networks that activates upon detecting an injected trigger. Most existing research assumes these triggers remain static in pattern and location, a property that significantly exposes the confidentiality of fine-tuning Fine-Tuning services.

Our investigation explores the feasibility of training neural network models via third-party services that utilize learning backdoor mechanisms where the trigger itself is updated, allowing the attacker to outsource the adjustment process without the initial model containing the injection.

Our approach enables updates to the hidden functionality of an attack mid-campaign through inversion techniques. This method allows the attacker to capture images of the trigger via remote access, ensuring the continuity of the breach, while the malicious user retains control of the target on a secure, local server.

Specifically, we develop two algorithms for attacking convolutional neural network (CNN) models using image cloud services with the above capability. These methods impose negligible additional costs during both training and validation, yet successfully produce potent backend traps. We demonstrate this efficacy through extensive experiments on (GTA) datasets and actual image cloud platforms, confirming the success of the attack against standard defense strategies.

High-precision astrometry relies on relativistic models of light propagation grounded in the parametrised post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, a framework used to investigate potential general relativistic violations in observational data. Among various PPN parameters, $\gamma$, which quantifies the deflection of light by gravity, significantly influences astrometric measurements. This study analyzes both theoretically and computationally how deviations of PPN $\gamma$ from its General Relativity value of unity impact parallax measurements in Gaia-like missions. By first examining the individual and combined astrometric effects of gravitational deflection and stellar image displacement—two phenomena that shift apparent positions—we derive the formula for parallax modulation due to these effects. Additionally, considering that Gaia measures stellar sizes rather than just point-like positions, we specifically address image displacement impacts. Finally, in light of current Gaia precision capabilities, we argue that systematic errors arising from PPN $\gamma$ deviations are too minor to compromise the mission's goals.

Utilizing external knowledge to assist machine-based question answering (QA) on tasks requiring commonsense background faces the challenge of overwhelming and misleading information due to the boundless volume of such data. To address this, we introduce a semantics-driven, knowledge-aware QA framework designed to regulate knowledge injection from coarse to fine granularity. We implement a filtering strategy to refine extracted information based on the initial (coarse) semantics of a question and have created a semantics-aware retrieval module. This module leverages structural knowledge inputs and performs hierarchical fusion of appropriate facts aligned with the precise (fine-grained) semantics of questions. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches on the CommonsenseQA benchmark dataset.

This work addresses the challenge where a Parameter Server and multiple data-rich client nodes must collaboratively train a statistical model, with each node holding private data that remains inaccessible to others. While the primary goal is to achieve model forecasting with high accuracy, secondary goals focus on minimizing the communication overhead between the server and nodes, as well as safeguarding each node's data privacy. We evaluate a series of statistical regression modeling algorithms designed to fulfill these requirements, testing their efficacy through extensive experiments in two scenarios: one where simulation handles data storage, and another utilizing real-world data. Our findings, particularly regarding communication efficiency and performance balance, highlight that specific algorithms offer distinct advantages, recommending further research into those offering the most optimized trade-offs between statistical accuracy and efficient use of resources.

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately experience mental health disorders. Drawing upon data from North Carolina courts covering 1994 to 2009, this study analyzes whether requiring offenders on probation to receive mental healthcare lowers their subsequent likelihood of reincarceration. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis contrasts individuals mandated to participate in treatment programs with those under probation without such requirements. The findings reveal that mandating treatment reduces recidivism within three years by a margin of 5.6 percentage points—or 17 percent—compared to non-treatment probationers. While specific impacts on violent and property crimes demonstrate reduced recurrence, the beneficial trends also intensify as time progresses post-conviction. Finally, a cost-benefit assessment indicates that resulting decreases in crime sufficiently reimburse expenses associated with offering these programs.

Pixel-level annotation shortages remain a common hurdle in medical segmentation. This paper proposes a novel regularization technique utilizing interpolation-based mixing to enhance semi-supervised medical segmentation. The method introduces consistency regularization that ensures partitioned interpolated images from two unlabeled sources remain consistent with interpolations derived from their respective segmentation masks representing them. This data-adaptive regularization specifically aids reducing overfitting among labeled examples with high confidence. Superiourity over adversarial learning or one trained with generative modeling is attained without need to perform other compute-heavy processes that their counterparts use, as this method does not incur the cost. Tests run on two public datasets — ACDC, MMWHS both showed that the suggested approach is in fact the best of choices among comparable approaches working in the field with supervised data. Measuring atomic disorder levels is vital for understanding how changes in local structural environments influence material performance and longevity. This study utilizes graph neural networks to establish a physically interpretable index for local disorder. This index characterizes the variety of immediate atomic arrangements as a smooth continuum ranging from solid to liquid states, evaluated relative to thermal fluctuations. We demonstrate this new approach across three representative cases with distinct disorder levels: solid-liquid interfaces, polycrystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries. Focusing specifically on aluminum, we illustrate how this method captures the spatiotemporal development of such boundaries, including a rigorous mathematical definition of the boundary separating order and disorder within space. Additionally, we identify physics-consistent gradients emerging from these continuous disorder maps to aid in evaluating and forecasting material behavior and potential failures. Collectively, our framework offers a conceptual and adaptable method for linking complicated local atomic architectures to broader material phenomena.

Given a parametric family $f(y|\theta)$ for $\theta \in \Omega$, let $\eta(\theta)$ represent a specific function and $G$ be an unknown mixing distribution. The objective is to estimate the expected value $E_G[\eta(\theta)] = \int \eta(\theta) dG(\theta)$ using a nonparametric approach, assuming random samples are drawn. From the resulting data, observations $(X_i, Y_i)$ for $1 \leq i \leq n$ are obtained where $X_i$ are independent identical draws and each $(X_i, Y_i)$ pair follows the joint distribution defined by $f$ and $G$. This paper examines the theoretical properties of estimator $\hat{\mu}_n^{GML}$, which is constructed via Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators applied to this nonparametric framework, specifically targeting the identification of $G$. The expected accuracy of this estimator is explored by considering the auxiliary problem where $G$ assumes a discrete form with support on $J$ points; furthermore, an application demonstrating the practical application of $\hat{\mu}_n^{GML}$ within this context is provided.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) applies students' historical interaction records to model their evolving knowledge states and predict their future learning outcomes. While deep learning-based approaches for KT have recently achieved significant advancements, the exact drivers behind these DL-KT models remain elusive, and their proper evaluation and analysis continue to be difficult tasks. Specifically, existing methods often struggle with and potentially overfit on imbalanced datasets, yet standard practices utilize inappropriate balanced metrics that mask the reality; thereby, traditional assessments may misrepresent their actual performance. To address these challenges, we introduce WAKT, a straightforward yet effective baseline based on an attention mechanism. WAKT incorporates data-centric refinements such as set-reordered and weighted embeddings, which enhance evaluation accuracy, as well as balanced assessment protocols specifically designed for KT. Empirical tests across standard benchmarks demonstrate that WAKT closely rivals the complex DL-KT models, confirming that it effectively tracks students' evolving proficiency despite overhead.

This work demonstrates that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses a closed range within the smooth function space $C^\infty(M)$ on any manifold $M$. Moreover, for any manifold $M$ lacking compact subcomponents, the operator $P$ demonstrates surjectivity on $C^\infty(M)$, with applications yielding to Helmholtz theory explored accordingly.

The version of the proof format adopted by the veriT SMT solver was initially showcased ten years ago following the first PxTP workshop. Since its inception, this format has fully evolved to the point where it supports various SMT applications, with other proof-producing solvers also generating files in this format. To secure a better direction for future advancements in this format, this article aims to solicit input from practitioners. To achieve that, it will examine the evolution history of the format as well as the pragmatic strategies used through its development while discussing the issues that may arise when other generating-proofs engines rely on the veriT proofs format.

Synchronous updates often reduce efficiency in cross-device federated learning, specifically as the pool of active clients expands. Nguyen et al., 2022 demonstrated with their approach, dubbed FedBuff, that incorporating asynchronous updates—including some degree of staleness—can resolve this issue. By adopting this method to scale training more effectively, the algorithm ensures privacy remains intact. In revisiting and extending this algorithm for use with the other asynchronous federated computations considered earlier, we also lift the standard assumptions on the bounded norm of gradient updates. Finally, the current work provides a thorough analysis of this adjusted approach in conditions characterized both in its training performance with delayed and stochastic data updates as in its non-stationarity risks.

Recent advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) have yield high performance intermediates, mapping acoustic inputs to linguistic features. Despite this, the size of these intermediates remains substantially larger than actual vocabulary, introducing memory overhead and runtime delays that hinder deployment on resource-limited devices. This paper proposes a novel technique, referred to as Intermediate Alphabet Compression (IAC), designed to reduce the dimensions of such mappings with out compromising recognition accuracy. Our approach successfully adapts widely used character-based end-to-end ASR systems by creating significantly more compact mappings between words and acoustic inputs. Tests conducted on the standard WikiText and CommonCrawl datasets demonstrate that the proposed Intermediates result in mappings that are 96% and 98.3% the size of original vocabulary, respectively, while maintaining comparable performance. Beyond efficient use of memory, computations are streamlined, leading to substantial improvements. We introduce a Temporal Difference (TD) learning approach designed to tackle the navigation challenges marine robots encounter in underwater settings. To enhance data efficiency and ensure compatibility with real-time operations, the method integrates Gaussian Process regression with an advanced rejection-sparing algorithm. While most current Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) techniques primarily concentrate on generating extensive pseudo-training data to improve performance, very few tackle the challenge of few-shot domain adaptation. This study redefines various GEC environments as distinct tasks and introduces a methodology that applies few-shot meta-learning for domain adaptation entirely without synthetic pseudo data. By leveraging large data sets from source domains as anchors, we aim to create initial model parameters that enable rapid adaptation to new, low-resource target domains. The regulation of protoplanetary disk evolution relies on analyzing how accretion rates scale with star and disk attributes; however, utilizing the distribution of these relations as a constraint on evolutionary models requires accurately accounting for accretion fluctuations. While this effect may be significant during embedded phases, it has often been considered minor in later stages. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) focuses on learning effective multi-agent strategies from collected historical data, playing a crucial role in preparing systems for real-world deployment. A prevalent practical challenge is that individual behavior policies generating joint agent trajectories often exhibit varying performance levels—for instance, mixing data from automated simulation bots with that from professional players. While previous offline MARL research primarily assumed all data shares a consistent performance level, this study explores the complexity arising from heterogeneous data quality. We introduce Equi-Agent Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, an framework ensuring stable agent properties by standardizing the environment and action spaces of offline experiences. This normalization allows agents to maintain consistent performance across different data sets with potentially distinct action vocabularies, effectively isolating performance disparities to the distribution level rather than the individual agent level. To validate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments in both multi-agent coordination and competitive domains, including a real-world scenario involving distributed power trading among robots controlling motion and actions. Our results demonstrate that EquiAgent significantly outperforms leading offline MARL methods. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongzhongzhou/EquiAgent.

Saturn's stratosphere near its poles experiences the cyclical emergence and disappearance of extensive, warm vorticities located beyond approximately 75 degrees latitude, reaching maximum intensity during winter and completely disappearing throughout spring. The extended exploration period provided by the Cassini mission enables infrared spectral analysis to map the development of the Northern Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV)—characterized by higher temperature extremes and significant hydrocarbon densities at millibar pressure ranges in both polar regions. Using Cassiss data that reveal similar but less intense features in the South Pole, we designate these southern counterparts the Southern Polar Vortex (SPV). Distinctively, the SPV exhibits broad temperature variability with marked spatial non-uniformities, contrasting sharply with the more consistent nature of the NPS; under these differences, we propose designating the Southern Polar Vortex "Southern Polar Vortex" to reflect these characteristics. We observe these formations early in the planetary winter, originating in the first few quarters of the southern hemisphere season, with growth continuing until the autumn equinox. Based on Cassini observations, the NPS has developed under conditions where the atmosphere remains unstabilized, allowing for significant vertical transport across the stratosphere; however, the underlying mechanisms responsible for the highly heterogeneous structure of the SP形成 require further investigation to understand the formation process driving the vortex's development.

Spectroscopic methods rely on the interplay between matter and light to reveal details about a sample's internal structure. Although various approaches detect either the light transmitted through or reflected from a sample, or even particles scattering photons, all such techniques can alternatively be represented by detecting the phase of interference between a test signal and a reference, as seen in heterodyne and homodyne configurations. Corresponding to these detection methods are two distinct forms of spectroscopic sensitivity: intensity sensitivity, which relies on varying sample characteristics like absorption to modulate combined signal and reference intensities, and phase (or interferometric, or heterodyne, or HR) sensitivity, where changes in the test light's amplitude or presence are detected against a reference due to effects such as sample absorption or phase shifts. While the latter has historically been termed "absorptometry," or more broadly "phase spectrometry," this manuscript outlines the fundamental principles, mathematical frameworks, and practical implementations of these diverse techniques. It further explores sample applications and contrasts these methods by highlighting their respective sensitivity profiles to demonstrate the unified nature of intensity and phase-based detection in this field, ultimately arguing for the advantages offered by phase sensitivity.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are now integral to many safety-critical computer vision tasks, such as automated driving and human-robot collaboration. To ensure these systems remain functional in real-world settings, it is essential to defend against hardware memory faults, which can corrupt a CNN's live data and cause incorrect or unsafe decisions. This study identifies activation clipping as an accessible and effective hardware technique that restricts numerical overflows without requiring complex memory verification. We conduct a thorough analysis of this method's robustness and recovery capabilities against various fault models. We also adapt the clipping technique for training phases to prepare neural networks to handle such limitations. Most significantly, we assess activations and parameters across several state-of-the-art CNNs utilized in safety-sensitive domains. The results confirm that activation clipping techniques position themselves as a viable solution for protecting safety-critical CNN inferences affected by memory faults.

We propose a multilingual common semantic space grounded in distributional semantics, enabling knowledge and resource sharing by projecting vocabulary from various languages into an integrated representation space that exceeds basic pairwise word alignment. To achieve this, we introduce multi-level cluster alignment strategies that utilize more abstract signals than distributional features to link computational clusters with linguistic clusters across different languages, thereby offering strong supervision. Specifically, we fuse structural clusters derived from syntactic parse trees and phraseology with semantic clusters from WordNet entries. The space is optimized through an iterative process involving two stages: initially, dimension reduction creates language-specific subspaces preserved as external fixes; subsequently, a unified dimension produces direct mappings from each language, which is refined to minimize discrepancies between imposed clusters on word contexts and preserved inter-cluster relationships. Evaluations demonstrate significant improvements over currently available multilingual word alignment methods.

ViDaExpert serves as a specialized utility for the visualization and analysis of multidimensional vectorial datasets. Designed to handle "object-feature" formatted tables—controlling both numerical attributes and textual row/column labels—it integrates a suite of statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Elastic Maps (offering a non-linear approach to PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and multilinear regression, alongside K-Means clustering and decision-tree construction variants.
